“Not a Single Minute”: Von der Leyen Slams Russia’s Ceasefire Violations as EU Prepares 22nd Sanctions Package
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union would not lift any sanctions against Russia until Moscow ends its war against Ukraine, accusing the Kremlin of escalating attacks instead of observing the energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump.
Speaking to journalists ahead of the second day of the European Council meeting in Brussels on October 16, von der Leyen said the EU was preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Of course, we supported President Trump's energy ceasefire, but we've seen that Russia did not respect it. Not a single minute. Instead, Russia escalated. And therefore, we have to increase the pressure on Russia. We're working now on the 22nd sanctions package. And one thing is absolutely clear. We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war,” von der Leyen stated.
Alongside efforts to increase economic pressure on Moscow, the European Commission president emphasized that the EU remains focused on helping Ukraine prepare for the upcoming winter, particularly as Russian attacks continue to threaten the country’s critical infrastructure.
“Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure. But we stand by your side. We will support you as we did it in the other winters. We will overcome,” von der Leyen said, addressing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The Commission president also outlined the broader agenda of the European Council meeting, noting that EU leaders would discuss Ukraine’s financial, budgetary, and military requirements, covering both 2026 and the following year.
Beyond immediate financial and military assistance, von der Leyen stressed the importance of Ukraine continuing its reform efforts as part of its European integration process. She urged Kyiv to maintain progress on reforms to enable the opening of the remaining negotiation clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession process by the end of the year.
Her remarks come as Ukraine continues to face extensive damage to its energy infrastructure following a series of Russian missile strikes, including a major attack on October 14.
According to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, Russian forces struck all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants during the attack, while also targeting critical energy facilities in Kharkiv and the surrounding region.
Koretskyi reported that Russian ballistic missiles had been deliberately directed at energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the Kharkiv region. Additional strikes hit essential facilities in the Kyiv region responsible for supplying electricity to the capital and central parts of Ukraine.

articles.title: Rubio heads to Central Asia as US seeks greater role in region dominated by Russia and China - Gazeta Express
articles.summary: Rubio heads to Central Asia as US seeks greater role in region dominated by Russia and China  Gazeta Express
articles.full_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Uzbekistan this weekend for talks with five Central Asian countries, as the Trump administration aims to strengthen trade ties and expand Washington's strategic presence in the region.
Rubio will participate in a ministerial meeting to be held from October 17 to 20 in Samarkand, as part of the C5+1 format, which brings together the United States with Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. He will also hold bilateral meetings with senior officials from the five countries and lead a trade delegation of more than 200 business leaders, the State Department announced on October 13.
The visit comes at a time when the US is showing growing interest in Central Asia's critical minerals, energy resources and transport corridors, as governments in the region seek to diversify partnerships and reduce dependence on traditional powers.
"This unprecedented engagement between the United States and the countries of Central Asia, as well as this visit, would constitute the first step towards this goal," said Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, in a statement to Radio Free Europe (RFE/RL).
"Central Asian countries are not all that happy with the idea of replacing Russian dominance with Chinese dominance," he said, explaining why the region's capitals are reaching out to Washington and European partners.
Russia's war against Ukraine has diverted Moscow's attention and resources from the region, creating opportunities for other powers to deepen ties with Central Asia.
Meanwhile, China has expanded its presence in the region through trade, infrastructure investment, and its flagship initiative, the Belt and Road.
“The Trump administration is focused primarily on its own interests, America’s interests, and global competition with China,” said Ariel Cohen, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and managing director of the Energy, Growth, and Security Program at the International Center for Taxation and Investment.
"It's clear that China is the dominant economic partner, while Russia continues to offer many security ties. But the United States is not backing down and abandoning this space," Cohen added.
Strengthening economic and diplomatic ties could help Washington secure supply chains, expand trade opportunities, and prevent a single power from gaining overwhelming influence across the region.
The planned delegation, with more than 200 business leaders, underscores the importance the administration places on trade diplomacy, analysts said. Washington hopes the closer engagement will lead to investment and business deals in a range of sectors, they said.
"We have already made tremendous progress in strengthening our relationships with Central Asian countries, and we must continue to expand these partnerships by removing outdated Soviet-era trade restrictions, known as Jackson-Vanik," Republican Senator Steve Daines told REL.
He referred to legislation that denies normal trade relations status to some current and former non-trading economies if they do not meet certain requirements regarding freedom of migration.
Critical minerals are an important part of this picture, but Central Asia's strategic value also stems from its position between China, Russia, South Asia, and Europe. Transport routes connecting the region to international markets have gained importance, as governments seek alternatives to routes that pass through Russia.
Moriyasu cited the Middle Corridor, which connects Central Asia to Europe via the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus, as part of the broader strategic opportunities. A stronger presence of American companies along these routes could help establish lasting American economic interests in the region.
The success of the visit will depend on whether the diplomatic momentum translates into concrete commitments for investment and continued trade cooperation, or whether it remains simply a high-profile meeting.
Organizing the meeting gives Uzbekistan the opportunity to strengthen relations with Washington and simultaneously raise its profile as a regional diplomatic hub.
President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has repeatedly sought rapprochement with the United States. According to preliminary information provided for this report, Washington has invited Mirziyoyev and Kazakhstan's President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev to attend the G20 summit, which will be held in Miami in December.
The diplomatic engagement has fueled speculation about a possible visit by President Donald Trump to Central Asia. Such a visit would be unprecedented for a sitting US president and could provide Washington with more sustained access to the region's leaders.
Laura Linderman, senior fellow at the American Foreign Policy Council and director of programs at the Central Asia and Caucasus Institute, said Rubio's participation in the C5+1 meeting was already a positive development.
She said that expanding the format to include Azerbaijan, creating a C6+1 framework, could make cooperation more ambitious.
"The event would be considered an even greater success if the US expanded the format to C6+1 and included Azerbaijan," Linderman told REL.
A senior Wall Street executive traveling with Rubio's delegation to Samarkand said that in decades of working with the region, he had never seen such strong interest from American businesses. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
"We know that there are close personal ties between members of the Trump administration and some Central Asian presidents. But the current interest in Uzbekistan and other countries in the region goes beyond these relations. It is both personal and institutional," he told REL.
According to the leader, the growing interest of American companies is also driven by the intensification of economic competition with China.
"American businesses have realized that if they don't increase their activities in the region, China will soon swallow everything there. They want to compete with China globally and right next to it, since the region is adjacent to it," he said.
After Uzbekistan, Rubio will travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar, India, for his second official visit to the country this year. He is expected to meet with government officials and business leaders to discuss the US-India strategic partnership, regional and global developments, energy cooperation and commercial investment./REL/

articles.title: DP World eyes $5 bn India investment, warns West Asia crisis is rewiring global trade - The Economic Times
articles.summary: DP World eyes $5 bn India investment, warns West Asia crisis is rewiring global trade  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Synopsis
DP World is ready to increase its investment in India between USD 3 billion and USD 5 billion in the coming years. The company urges for faster infrastructure development and quicker project approvals to unlock trade potential. Despite challenges, Narayan believes that India remains attractive due to its growing economic scale. Enhanced logistics capacity is critical for supporting India's manufacturing and export growth.
"We are prepared to invest between USD 3 billion and USD 5 billion (in India)," he told a select group of journalists.
"If Vadhavan happens, what do you think Vadhavan is going to cost? In phases, in different phases, it will be USD 10 billion of investment," he said, referring to the scale of the proposed port development over 10 to 15 years.
DP World, which has built an integrated Indian network spanning ports, rail and inland logistics, is seeking to expand its footprint as the world's most populous country looks to strengthen domestic connectivity and become a larger manufacturing and export hub.
The company announced an additional USD 5 billion India investment commitment in October 2025, over and above USD 3 billion invested in the country over three decades.
India's infrastructure push has delivered substantial improvements, Narayan said, but port and rail development and the processes governing project execution need to move faster.
"One always hopes things could happen faster," he said, pointing to the long wait for the Vadhavan project and arguing that infrastructure development should keep pace with progress in roads, airports and power.
DP World is prepared to bid for new opportunities, expand its rail network and increase port capacity, Narayan said. The company currently operates six port concessions in India and plans to increase its railheads from eight to 12, according to him.
India's growing economic scale makes it attractive despite historically weaker returns on invested capital, Narayan said. Currency depreciation, driven in part by the country's energy import bill, has weighed on returns, while infrastructure upgrades, digitisation and the shift towards renewable energy could improve the outlook.
The proposed investment would also help strengthen DP World's wider supply-chain network, rather than simply expand its Indian business, he said.
The investment push comes as disruptions around key West Asian maritime chokepoints force shipping companies to reroute cargo, add capacity and absorb higher operating costs.
The impact extends beyond the port itself, he said, because Jebel Ali serves as a major transshipment hub linking Asian manufacturing centres with markets in the Middle East, Africa and Europe.
DP World had expected Jebel Ali's port operations to generate about USD 1.2 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), but Narayan said the disruption would materially reduce the group's earnings outlook. He estimated that global EBITDA could fall to about USD 5.8 billion from a level of roughly USD 6.2 billion to USD 6.4 billion, with growth elsewhere cushioning part of the lost contribution.
The company is exploring alternative routes through other Gulf ports and overland connections, including routes through Saudi Arabia, Narayan said. But building replacement capacity takes time, and he estimated that new port capacity could take two to three years to develop.
"Port capacity is not created overnight," he said, warning that the full consequences of the disruption may take time to emerge.
The crisis also underscores the growing cost of building redundancy into supply chains. Companies that once prioritised lean inventories, low costs and just-in-time deliveries are increasingly seeking alternative suppliers, routes and production centres to reduce their exposure to geopolitical shocks.
Narayan said global trade now required substantially more shipping capacity to move less cargo than before, as longer routes and operational inefficiencies absorbed available capacity. Higher interest rates, fuel expenses and other operating costs were adding to the burden.
"Who do you think pays for all this disruption? You - as a consumer," he said, arguing that the additional costs would ultimately be passed through to buyers of goods.
He expects shorter supply chains and a greater emphasis on regional production to reshape trade flows over time, potentially increasing the importance of north-south trade between Asia, Africa and other emerging markets.
For India, the opportunity lies in expanding manufacturing and exports while building the port, rail and inland logistics infrastructure needed to connect producers with global markets.
Narayan said India's exports and imports currently account for a relatively small share of its overall economy, leaving considerable room for growth. A substantial increase in trade would require a corresponding expansion in logistics capacity, he said.
However, he cautioned that resilience would come at a cost. Maintaining alternative routes, suppliers and inventory buffers would make supply chains more expensive and capital-intensive than the lean systems businesses had previously pursued.
"The world has to come to peace," Narayan said, arguing that physical infrastructure alone cannot eliminate the risks posed by conflict.

articles.title: Why Losing a Taiwan War Might Not Break China - The National Interest
articles.summary: Why Losing a Taiwan War Might Not Break China  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
The Yuan dynasty felt secure enough to invade Japan—and suffer catastrophic losses—because its position on the Eurasian landmass was secure. Is China’s today?
Many Western analysts believe that a failed Taiwan operation could threaten Communist rule in China and that Chinese Communist Party General Secretary Xi Jinping therefore would not risk everything on such a high-stakes gamble. This hypothesis may or may not be true. But China’s own imperial history suggests another possibility. Over seven centuries ago, Kublai Khan, Great Khan of the Mongols and emperor of China’s Yuan Dynasty, launched two massive amphibious invasions of Japan. Both ended in failure. Yet Kublai remained on the throne, and the Yuan Dynasty survived for nearly another century. Why? Because the defeat at sea did not destroy the Yuan’s continental foundations of power.
Today, the People’s Republic of China under Xi has approached its near-environs in Eurasia and the Pacific with a strikingly similar logic. That Xi hopes to bolster China’s power in the Pacific is hardly a secret. Yet under an increasingly continental conception of strategy, Beijing is also building sources of power that extend far into the Asian landmass. The United States and its allies need to grasp this continental dimension of Chinese power, so as not to overlook the larger strategic system that could allow Beijing to take risks at sea.
The Mongol Empire was first forged on the high steppe under Genghis Khan, and consolidated in China under his grandson Kublai Khan. Kublai ruled China as emperor of the Yuan Dynasty (1271–1368), establishing his capital in present-day Beijing. It was under the Yuan that the far-flung regions of Tibet and Yunnan were brought under Chinese rule. At the same time, the Yuan Emperor, as Great Khan, claimed nominal supremacy over the other Mongol khanates ruled by members of his extended family: the Golden Horde in what is now southern Russia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, and the Ilkhanate centered on Iran. Together with tributary and vassal relationships extending into Korea and parts of Southeast Asia, this gave the Yuan court a political horizon that stretched far beyond China proper, deep into the Eurasian continent.
The Han-led Ming Dynasty, which succeeded the Yuan in 1368, cast the Mongols as barbarians and rhetorically distanced itself from their rule. Yet in strategic practice, the continental focus the Yuan brought to Chinese foreign relations endured. Yongle, the Ming’s third emperor, repeatedly led armies deep into Mongolia, competing with the descendants of Genghis Khan to shape the balance of power across the Eurasian steppe.
Modern China’s behavior echoes this continental strategic logic. Like the Ming, the rhetoric of Xi’s China has hedged towards a promotion of Han nationalism. However, like the Yuan before it, the modern Chinese state has devoted enormous resources to securing its land frontiers, strengthening political and economic ties across Central Asia, and building infrastructure that binds China more closely to the Eurasian interior. In both the medieval and modern cases, security on the Asian continent provides the strategic depth that allows the Chinese state to devote greater attention and resources to its maritime periphery.
Divine Winds, Medieval and Modern
In War on the Rocks, we argued that Eurasia, not just the Indo-Pacific, will be crucial to the next phase of Taiwan deterrence. We focused on the trade and energy corridors that China is building across the Eurasian landmass, as well as Beijing’s engagement with crucial swing states along those routes. Pipelines and railways traversing the continent are less vulnerable to US maritime power than maritime routes, and could provide China with alternative economic and energy lifelines in a contingency such as a war over Taiwan.
The Belt and Road Initiative’s overland component is oriented toward Inner Asia and evokes the Silk Road caravans of the 13th-century Pax Mongolica, when Mongol rule facilitated the movement of merchants, goods, technologies, and ideas across much of Eurasia. Under Kublai, Beijing sat at the eastern end of a vast political and commercial network extending through Mongol-ruled territories far into the continental interior.
Why does this matter for Taiwan? Kublai offers a history lesson.
In the late 13th century, the Yuan launched naval expeditions as far afield as Japan and Java as Kublai sought to extend his authority beyond China’s shores. It was the failed invasions of Japan, during which storms devastated the Yuan-led fleets, that gave rise to the Japanese legend of the kamikaze, or “divine wind”—later lending its name to the notorious World War II suicide attacks, but predating them by centuries.
To prepare for the invasions, Kublai mustered thousands of soldiers and sailors for both the 1274 campaign and the far larger second campaign in 1281. Korea supplied much of the fleet for the first invasion, while in 1281 Yuan forces launched a two-pronged assault on southern Japan involving Chinese and Korean ships and troops. Kublai’s secure position on the Asian mainland gave him the strategic depth to undertake these expeditions at enormous cost in personnel and materiel.
Logistical difficulties, Japanese resistance, storms, and the inherent limitations of premodern warfare ultimately thwarted Kublai’s ambitions against the shogunate. Yet the very fact that he could mount two such expeditions demonstrates both the resources at his command and the importance the Yuan attached to the effort. Despite these military failures, the dynasty survived for nearly another century. Its collapse in the late 14th century was not due to the sorts of major military invasions that had featured in its rise, but rather to popular rebellions that arose from domestic mismanagement.
Ultimately, the Yuan was able to sponsor significant overseas campaigns against Japan and survive their failure because it could absorb the losses without jeopardizing its position at home. It was the preeminent continental power in Eurasia, with no significant rivals capable of threatening its northern Chinese heartland.
Seven centuries later, the Communist Party today has staked much of its political capital on the promise of “reunifying” the Chinese nation, tying that goal to Xi’s broader project of national “rejuvenation.” Taiwan occupies a far more central place in the Chinese Communist Party’s conception of sovereignty and national rejuvenation than Kublai’s Japan campaigns, which were about imperial expansion. A defeat over Taiwan would therefore carry political stakes far greater than those of Kublai’s failures.
Yet extraordinary shocks do not necessarily produce regime change. The Chinese Communist Party has already survived civil war, world war, the Cultural Revolution, and the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests. It should not be assumed that a failed Taiwan operation would automatically trigger regime collapse in China.
Disrupting the “Khanate” in Inner Asia
Modern China differs from Mongol China in another way. Unlike the Yuan Dynasty, which sat at the center of a broader political order across Eurasia, today’s China must actively compete with the United States and other powers for influence across the continent. While we offer a broader set of recommendations for strengthening that competition in our War on the Rocks piece, here we propose a narrower set of administrative changes within the US government. The objective is to place Central Asia at the heart of America’s China strategy.
Our first recommendation is to move military responsibility for the five Central Asian republics—Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Tajikistan—from the US Central Command (CENTCOM) to the newly-renamed US Pacific Command (USPACOM). All five currently fall under CENTCOM, lumped in with the greater Middle East from Egypt to Pakistan. It is time to stop viewing Central Asia primarily through the legacy of US operations in Afghanistan and instead see the region through the prism of long-term strategic competition with China. Making the USPACOM commander responsible for Central Asia would integrate the region into planning for Pacific contingencies and encourage planners to consider how developments along China’s continental periphery could affect Beijing’s calculations over Taiwan.
Second, the undersecretary of defense for policy should shift responsibility for the five Central Asian republics to the assistant secretary for Indo-Pacific security affairs—and establish a dedicated office for Central Asia and Mongolia, headed by a deputy assistant secretary for Inner Asian affairs. A new Inner Asia office would consolidate expertise and give the region an institutional advocate able to assess Central Asia not simply as an adjunct to other theaters, but as a strategic arena in its own right.
Third, the same logic should extend to the State Department and Congress. At State, Central Asia should be severed from the Bureau of South and Central Asian Affairs and brought into the bureau responsible for East Asia and the Pacific, aligning the diplomatic and defense bureaucracies around the same strategic geography. Congress should similarly pair Central Asia with East Asia and the Pacific rather than South Asia. Washington needs to adapt to the geopolitical reality that Central Asia is no longer primarily an adjunct to stabilizing Afghanistan, and is strategically distinct from the maritime-oriented Indian subcontinent: it is increasingly part of the China challenge, and must be treated accordingly.
If the United States wants to deter a modern Chinese maritime campaign against Taiwan, it should draw a lesson from medieval China’s maritime failures more than 700 years ago. articles.title: Teen in Kazakhstan Develops AI Sign Language Translator - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Teen in Kazakhstan Develops AI Sign Language Translator  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Fifteen-year-old Sanzhar Yerezhepov is developing an artificial intelligence (AI) translator to make online information more accessible to deaf people in Kazakhstan. Called Tusin (“Understand”), the platform converts speech and text into lifelike sign language videos that reproduce facial expressions as well as hand movements.
Yerezhepov attends Daryn, a specialized school for gifted children in Kokshetau, northern Kazakhstan. A boarding school for children with hearing and speech impairments is located nearby. Watching its students communicate in sign language made him wonder how easily they could access information online, giving him the idea for Tusin.
Yerezhepov is from Shiyeli, a small village in Kazakhstan’s Burabay district. Neither of his parents works in science or IT.
He is now working with the Kazakhstan Society of the Deaf to test an early version of Tusin and says five organizations have expressed willingness to work with him. The project reached the semifinals of an IT competition at Astana Hub, Kazakhstan’s international technology park for startups.
In an interview with The Times of Central Asia, Yerezhepov explains why translating into sign language is more complicated than adding subtitles. He discusses the medical startup he put on hold and what he hopes to change in Kazakhstan’s education system.
TCA: Tusin translates online content into sign language, but many videos already have subtitles. Why are those sometimes not enough for deaf viewers?
Yerezhepov: For some deaf people, especially those whose primary language is sign language, understanding written text can be difficult. First, subtitles are not always available in a language they are comfortable with. They are often automatically generated and do not convey information accurately. Second, sign language has its own grammar and structure. So even someone living in Kazakhstan may have difficulty understanding subtitles in Kazakh or Russian. Many deaf people can read subtitles fluently, but others need sign language translation.
TCA: Isn’t sign language the same around the world?
Yerezhepov: No. Different countries use different sign languages. There is no single universal sign language that everyone on Earth understands.
TCA: So which sign language is used in Kazakhstan?
Yerezhepov: Kazakhstan, like some other former Soviet countries, uses Russian Sign Language. We do not have a separate Kazakh Sign Language, although some signs have been adapted.
TCA: How do you teach artificial intelligence to understand and reproduce signs? Who checks its work?
Yerezhepov: We work with representatives of the Akmola branch of the Kazakhstan Society of the Deaf and with sign language interpreters. Together, we examine each sign, check how accurately it is reproduced, and analyze the results. We have already demonstrated our technology to deaf and hard-of-hearing people, and they understand what the platform communicates.
TCA: A sign can change meaning depending on the situation. How does Tusin handle that?
Yerezhepov: Quite well, although we are still working on it. The same sign can have different meanings depending on the context. That is exactly the problem we are addressing with artificial intelligence, which can take context into account and determine what is being communicated. Our platform also generates photorealistic videos that convey facial expressions and emotions, which are a very important part of sign language.
TCA: The Kazakhstani app SignBridge uses 3D avatars. Why did you decide to focus on photorealistic video?
Yerezhepov: During customer development, or research into whether potential customers need a product and are willing to pay for it, we discovered that ordinary 3D avatars do not always convey sign language accurately enough. As I mentioned, the same sign can have several meanings, so you also need to pay attention to emotions and facial expressions, and 3D models do not reproduce them well enough. That is why we focused on photorealism. There is currently no comparable product in the Commonwealth of Independent States market that pays this much attention to that aspect.
TCA: Will Tusin support other languages as you expand across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS)? What about English?
Yerezhepov: For now, we are working with Kazakh and Russian. Once we scale up the project in Kazakhstan, we plan to enter the CIS market and gradually add Central Asian languages. Russian Sign Language will remain the main sign language because, as I mentioned, it is used in several CIS countries. Our system can also recognize spoken English, but it will translate it into Russian Sign Language. If we eventually enter the international market, we will be able to add other sign languages, such as British and American Sign Language.
TCA: Are similar technologies already available abroad?
Yerezhepov: Yes, there is already a similar startup operating in the British market. It also emphasizes photorealism and uses the sign languages used in Britain and America. We studied its experience, and it inspired us.
TCA: Do you think you might compete with it someday?

TCA: Who might use Tusin first?

It could be almost anyone. For example, television news channels are required to provide sign language interpretation for one of their daily news programs. Or transportation organizations: bus operators, railway stations, and airports, where important announcements are often made only over loudspeakers, without accompanying text. Private companies could also adopt our technology. Banks, for example, could use our platform at terminals and customer service locations.
TCA: Businesses in Kazakhstan are not required to translate all their information into sign language. What might persuade companies to pay for such a service?
Yerezhepov: Kazakhstan’s legislation does not currently require all private companies to provide sign language interpretation for their information. But quite recently, on September 7, 2026, sign language was officially recognized in Kazakhstan’s Social Code as an independent language system. We hope additional requirements for information accessibility will eventually be introduced. But demand for our product depends not only on legislation. It also depends on how much companies care about their reputation and social responsibility. For example, Freedom pays attention to inclusivity and making its services accessible to people with hearing and speech impairments. There are other examples, too. Experts estimate that there could be between 150,000 and 200,000. The World Federation of the Deaf estimates that approximately 70 million people use sign language.

They helped us develop the project, organized meetings where we analyzed our decisions, introduced us to different people, and helped us build useful connections.

I won a silver medal at the regional stage of the Republican Informatics Olympiad and also participated in the national finals. This year, I won a bronze medal in the Applied Science category at Infomatrix Asia 2026, an international competition for school students in computing and innovation.

UPDATE 1624 GMT:
Pope Leo XIV has appealed to Vladimir Putin for a ceasefire allowing the delivery of food and medical assistance into Russian-occupied Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
Expressing his “grave concern”, the Pope asked for voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population of the city in the Kherson region.
Oleshky had a pre-invasion population of 24,000. Around 2,000 civilians, including 50 children, remain in the city and its surrounding villages.
Residents have sent messages that they are eating weeds in an effort to survive.
Ukrainian military authorities have attempted airdrops of emergency food, water, and medical supplies with large drones. It is unclear how much of the aid has been intercepted by the Russian military.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says that he sees “no willingness on the Russian side to end this war”.

[This is] the only means Ukraine has to signal to Russia that it is prepared to defend itself.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has asked the European Union for another €70 billion ($79 billion) next year to fund Ukraine’s defense against Russia.
Zelensky told EU leaders that the war will cost €155 billion ($174 billion) in 2027: “And we need at least €70 billion more from you – for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount.”
UPDATE 1431 GMT:

Putin will listen to America if America really turns up the heat on him and makes one thing clear: either he chooses peace or he gets no more money for his war.
UPDATE 1412 GMT:
Asked about Donald Trump’s attacks on him, including that he is supposedly more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky said:
I’m only standing up for Ukraine’s interests. And no matter how Russia would like to limit all of our rights, it’s clear that we do have a right to defend ourselves.
He explained that Vladimir Putin “does not seek negotiations in any format” but only “playing these games of words”: “He does not want the war to end.”
Zelensky asked about the Trump diesel deal with Russia, which could be followed by gas agreements or other attempts to lift sanctions on Russia or its frozen assets, “If I don’t stand up to this, if I don’t defend it, who else will do this diplomatically?”
He continues that Russia’s demands are not just about territory but about “our country’s existence”. Putin “wants to destroy us” and “does not respect our sovereignty and territorial integrity”.
The President summarized, “We’re now standing and fighting. What’s the alternative? Annihilation.”
UPDATE 1144 GMT:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken about air defense and the White House’s restrictions on Starshield, the military service of Starlink.
He said of the critical situation with air defense interceptors, “We are picking them up where we can: one or two here, five there, ten there, arranging all of this and bringing them to Ukraine.”
Zelensky said Ukraine’s requests for further help are “the bare minimum” needed. He was confident that European countries have enough interceptors to share and “go through this winter”.
He said that Starshield has been restored, but not yet to previous speeds needed for the frontline and air defenses.
Starlink was not turned off, but the speed limits were lowered…and we were incapable of shooting down some Shahed drones, and were no longer able to use one of the tools to protect our population.
Jet-powered Shaheds move at 400 km/h, he noted, and the Starshield speed limits were reduced to 70 km/h.
Our Defense ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities. Have they returned the previous, previous, speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.
UPDATE 1130 GMT:
Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar has commented on his first meeting with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Magyar replaced the pro-Kremlin Viktor Orbán, who had led Hungary the previous 12 years, after victory in April’s Parliamentary elections.
Magyar welcomed the Ukrainian Parliament’s adoption of a new law on minority education, including for ethnic Hungarians, as “a first step towards restoring mutual trust”. He said the two sides will “continue consultations … at the ministerial level”: “We agreed that it is in the interest of both countries to place their political and economic relations on a new foundation.”
Magyar declared his solidarity with Zelensky “in the face of inhumane Russian aggression against his country”: “Hungary stands ready to provide assistance, through all available diplomatic means, towards achieving an immediate ceasefire and a lasting peace.”
UPDATE 1124 GMT:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed his meeting, at the European Union summit, with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Zelensky cited the latest Russian attacks, including the murder of two civilians and injuring of 17 in Kharkiv city.
Right now, there are no signals from Russia that it is ready to end its war. The signals it is sending point to something entirely different and certainly do not bring peace any closer….
European leadership is needed to ensure that people’s lives are sufficiently protected from this Russian terror.
Zelensky cited discussions on air defense, energy, financial resilience, and Ukraine’s candidacy for EU membership.
UPDATE 0853 GMT:
At least three civilians have been murdered and seven injured in Ukraine’s second city Kharkiv by Russian strikes.
Around 370,000 customers lost power in the Volyn region in western Ukraine as Russia damaged civilian and critical infrastructure facilities.
Ukraine’s air defenses intercepted 114 of 149 drones fired by Russia overnight. Strikes were recorded at 24 locations.
UPDATE 0846 GMT:
Ukraine’s supply of Patriot interceptor missiles is critically low, say Kyiv’s officials.
One said “only a couple” of Patriot missiles remain, after an October 7 supply of ten was depleted to counter Russian attacks on Kyiv. Another said there are no missiles at all.

Arriving with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at a European Union leaders’ meeting in Brussels, European Council President António Costa said the EU’s support to Ukraine “remains as strong as ever”.
In an implicit message to the Trump Administration, Costa made clear:
This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions.
This is essential to bring Russia to accept a real ceasefire, to bring Russia to the table of negotiations and to stop this war.
He said to Zelensky, “You can count on us not only to support you in war, but most important for your future as a member of the European Union.”

Professor Maurice Okoli, Ph.D*
Perhaps, BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), with the new members and partner states, summit in New Delhi, on September 11 to13, produced a new round of significant declarations, adapting its collective policy towards an increasingly emerging architecture, while distinctively building an ‘Asian model’ of economic alliance. Under the chairmanship of India, the summit centered on creating a genuine reputation that has accumulated for nearly two decades. The timing was, particularly, notable. The most important strategic message was coined: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability.”
Addressing the BRICS summit of leading developing nations in New Delhi, Indian Prime Minister, Narendra Modi, warned rising geopolitical tensions, could increasingly affect people worldwide, and called for deepening cooperation and strengthening support across the Global South. “The number of conflicts and tensions in the world is continuously increasing, and this is having an increasingly negative and far-reaching impact on the lives of ordinary people,” Modi said, alongside with leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. That was one of the main messages sent across the world. Founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, BRICS has expanded to 11 members representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. It has sought greater representation for developing countries in global institutions and promoted alternative actions to Western-dominated financial systems.
Geopolitics: Is BRICS Challenging the West?
BRICS leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration, expressing indispensable concern relating to forging consensus over many strategic questions, backed greater use of local currencies in trade and stronger cross-border payment systems, while calling for cooperation on food security, energy, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and climate action. The declaration was a significant breakthrough, which holds competing positions on key regional and geopolitical issues–posed a complex diplomatic challenge amid ongoing conflicts and heightened geopolitical tensions. It emphasizes collective support for a multipolar world order and operational and structural reforms, at the United Nations, including its Security Council, as well as global financial institutions such as the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The declaration demonstrated BRICS can move together and act on multilateral economic cooperation, and its sustainability in Global South. That makes the question whether India has used its presidency to drum home for BRICS grouping to become more capable of taking economic action, with reports indicating that India entered a particular moment with more than just diplomatic presence. For instance, during the financial year 2024-25, its total exports amounted, approximately, $825 billion, with services accounting for an estimated $387 billion. Few developing countries can match New Delhi’s economic leverage, which stems from its large domestic market, expansion of digital economy, and sustainable growth. Despite national preferences and differences between BRICS members, it is worthy to note that India is a major provider of digital public infrastructure, and its demography plays an increasingly important role in global consumption, production, and services. It therefore exemplifies BRICS members have to build economic prosperity by opening doors. This new phase must strategically focus on a broader economic leverage. And appropriately, India’s geography provides an additional layer of economic leverage, which serves as a classical example for other Asian countries.
Сorporate Economic Weight, Limited Collective Power
While BRICS’s economic weight is enormous–its ability to wield it collectively is not, some analysts argued. However, experts’ arguments closely connected to BRICS operational successes and achievements should not only be measured by whether it can pose an alternative to multinational institutions, but also whether it could make any noticeable difference, in terms of using its natural resources to increase regional trade, raise economic production and improve distribution across the Global South. Several experts position portrays BRICS has offered its member countries alternative pathways for channeling trade and investment that serve the collective interests of member countries–largely national development and poverty alleviation.
Meanwhile, scholars have reminded that BRICS emerged after the 2008 financial collapse and the failures of the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) Doha Round–trade negotiations aimed at reforming the international trading system in favour of Global South countries. Why would the BRICS want to take on the global governance responsibilities of the G7 members? This has been the basic question among scholars until today. It is, however, believed that reforms and greater autonomy would be a greater concern for BRICS rather than overthrowing the unravelling liberal international order.
BRICS+ Financial Architecture
The group is noticeably dominated by China, which has the largest share of the group’s GDP, accounting to about 70% of the organization total. The financial architecture of BRICS is made of the New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA). These components were signed into a treaty in 2014 and became active in 2015. The New Development Bank (NDB), formally referred to as the BRICS Development Bank, is a multilateral development bank operated by the five BRICS states. It has non-members as contributors to the NDB.
The bank’s primary focus of lending is infrastructure projects with authorized lending of up to $34 billion annually. South Africa hosts the African headquarters of the bank. The bank has a starting capital of $50 billion, with wealth increased to $100 billion over time. Records show Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa initially contributed $10 billion each to bring the total to $50 billion. As of 2020, it had 53 projects underway worth around $15 billion. By 2025, the bank had approved more than $32 billion for 96 projects.
In 2021, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates and Uruguay joined the NDB. With India’s presidency in 2026, which was estimated to be a comprehensive and promising for BRICS, as India has outlined its framework of priorities, as it did during its G20 presidency several years ago. In close-coordination with members and partner-states within the BRICS, India has ensured the balance of multifaceted interests, and established mutual-trust in the multipolar world system. The goal of transforming into a full-fledged international organization must go beyond addressing current geopolitical challenges, the necessity to develop effective ways of engaging in global development to reflect multipolarity. Today, collectively, BRICS comprises more than a quarter of the global economy and nearly half the world’s population.
BRICS Advocates for Reforms at Financial Institutions
Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of BRICS countries have called for reform of global developmental financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, seeking a stronger voice for emerging market economies. “We will continue to strengthen coordination among BRICS members to make international financial institutions more representative, transparent and accountable. With the growing share of emerging market and developing economies in global output and growth, reform of global economic governance remains a consistent BRICS priority,” Finance Chiefs of BRICS countries underlined in an official joint statement.
“We continue to have serious concerns with the unilateral imposition of trade and finance-related actions, including the raising of tariffs and non-tariff measures, which distort trade and are inconsistent with World Trade Organisation rules,” the statement said. “We encourage the BRICS Payment Task Force to continue discussions, building on the ongoing work, to facilitate practical solutions for cross-border payments among BRICS countries, which are fast, low-cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent, and safe,” the statement said. While acknowledging the work done by the BRICS payment task force, the finance chiefs pushed for progress in ensuring greater interoperability of payment systems across member nations. It further noted India will push for progress on linking digital currencies across BRICS countries.
BRICS-Africa Transiting from Diplomacy to Strategic Economy
South Africa (2010), Ethiopia and Egypt (2024), as fully-fledged BRICS members, are seemingly changing policy which has always been strategic ambiguity, to a kind of assertive flexibility. South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt are positioning also as leading African voices for the Global South while, at the same time, maintaining relationships with competing Western powers. In principles, Africa generally collaborates with the United States and Asian-Pacific partners while striking, to a certain degree, multifaceted ties with Russia, and operates within framework of BRICS domain.
South African Cyril Ramaphosa, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of Arab Republic of Egypt held separate conversations on the current status and future prospects for their relations, and further discussed ways of strengthening BRICS strategic partnership in politics and security, economics and finance, and cultural and humanitarian ties, while exchanging divergent views on current international and regional issues that are of common significance to the global development. South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt, however, plan to take new initiatives to improve and strengthen relations within BRICS.

A $1 billion trade target is back on the agenda. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have reaffirmed their intention to expand bilateral trade turnover to that level following talks between Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Ilham Aliyev in Baku on October 15, 2026. According to the official statement from Akorda, the leaders also discussed energy exports, transport infrastructure and the newly launched Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Line, DKNews.kz reports.
The meeting highlighted the increasingly broad scope of Kazakhstan-Azerbaijan cooperation, with economic priorities extending from trade and energy to digital connectivity, logistics and regional diplomacy.
Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan target $1 billion in bilateral trade
Tokayev and Aliyev welcomed the positive momentum in economic relations and reaffirmed their shared objective of increasing bilateral trade turnover to $1 billion.
The target reflects a broader effort to deepen commercial ties between two countries located on opposite shores of the Caspian Sea.
Trade expansion is closely connected to cooperation in manufacturing, agriculture, transport and energy. Progress in these sectors could create additional opportunities for companies operating in both markets.
However, Akorda's statement did not specify a deadline for reaching the $1 billion target or provide updated bilateral trade figures.
The distinction matters: the presidents confirmed an existing strategic objective rather than announcing that the target had already been achieved.
Energy exports through Azerbaijan remain a priority
Another major subject of the talks was the potential expansion of Kazakh energy supplies through Azerbaijan.
For Kazakhstan, developing additional export routes is an important part of diversifying access to international markets.
Azerbaijan's position on the western shore of the Caspian Sea makes it a relevant partner for transport and energy connections linking Central Asia with the South Caucasus and beyond.
The presidents also reviewed prospects for joint projects in several sectors:
- Industry and manufacturing cooperation.
- Energy production and transportation.
- Transport and international logistics.
- Agriculture and related business opportunities.
No new shipment volumes, project investment amounts or implementation deadlines were announced in the official account of the meeting.
A new digital corridor across the Caspian Sea
The two presidents placed particular emphasis on the launch of the Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Line, a major telecommunications project connecting Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.
The infrastructure is designed to strengthen digital connectivity between the countries while providing an additional route for international data transmission between Europe and Asia.
According to the presidential statement, the project is expected to diversify digital corridors and create new opportunities for the wider region.
Its significance extends beyond telecommunications. The initiative adds a digital component to the broader system of transport and economic links being developed across the Caspian.
For Kazakhstan, additional international connectivity could support the development of cloud services, technology infrastructure and data-intensive industries.
For Azerbaijan, it creates further opportunities to participate in the digital networks connecting Central Asia with European markets.
Why the Caspian connection matters strategically
The Caspian Sea has become a central element of Kazakhstan-Azerbaijan cooperation because it connects several economic priorities at once.
Transport routes across the region support international freight movement. Energy infrastructure provides opportunities for exporting resources, while fiber-optic networks enable cross-border data transmission.
These projects serve different purposes but share a common geographic foundation: connecting Central Asia with the South Caucasus and European markets.
For Kazakhstan, cooperation with Azerbaijan can provide additional options for international trade and connectivity.
For Azerbaijan, closer ties with Kazakhstan strengthen its economic links with Central Asia.
However, the practical benefits will depend on infrastructure capacity, investment decisions, commercial demand and the implementation of existing agreements.
Tokayev acknowledges Azerbaijan's role in CICA
The meeting also addressed regional diplomacy and Azerbaijan's chairmanship of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA).
President Tokayev thanked President Aliyev for the invitation to the summit and for Azerbaijan's traditional hospitality.
He also praised the organization of the event and highlighted Azerbaijan's contribution to advancing CICA's agenda during its chairmanship.
According to Akorda, Tokayev specifically acknowledged efforts to promote practical initiatives and strengthen the organization's international standing.
This diplomatic dimension shows that Kazakhstan-Azerbaijan relations involve not only bilateral economic projects but also cooperation within broader Asian multilateral frameworks.
Education, tourism and parliamentary cooperation
Beyond trade and infrastructure, the leaders discussed the continued development of cultural and humanitarian ties.
Both sides noted progress in educational cooperation, tourism and interparliamentary engagement.
These areas contribute to the broader relationship by creating opportunities for contacts between institutions, businesses and citizens.
Educational cooperation can support academic exchanges and institutional partnerships, while tourism helps strengthen direct connections between the two societies.
The official statement did not announce specific new educational programmes, tourism agreements or numerical targets in these areas.
What the meeting means for Kazakhstan
The Baku talks reaffirmed the main priorities of Kazakhstan's strategic partnership with Azerbaijan.
Economically, the two countries continue to pursue the $1 billion bilateral trade target. In energy, Kazakhstan is exploring opportunities to expand supplies through Azerbaijani territory.
In transport and digital infrastructure, the emphasis is on strengthening connections across the Caspian Sea and creating additional routes between Asia and Europe.
These priorities reflect a relationship increasingly shaped by practical infrastructure and commercial cooperation alongside diplomatic engagement.
At the conclusion of the meeting, Tokayev and Aliyev reaffirmed their commitment to deepening the strategic partnership and consistently implementing agreements across the bilateral agenda.
The next measure of progress will be the extent to which these commitments translate into expanded trade, energy shipments and operational infrastructure projects.
Earlier, we reported on the major projects bringing Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan closer together, including the $1 billion trade objective, the Trans-Caspian transport route, energy cooperation and the fiber-optic connection across the Caspian Sea. The latest presidential meeting reaffirmed these priorities at the highest political level.

articles.title: Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Kyiv, Ukraine – The supernova-like blasts of exploding Russian ballistic missiles are followed by thunderous thumps, shockwaves, fires and deaths – and the staccato of Ukrainian air defence systems.
This week’s nightly attacks on Ukraine that killed at least 15 and wounded dozens resembled hundreds of previous raids – with one exception.
The air raid sirens began howling just seconds before or after yet another wave of missiles struck apartment buildings, power plants and warehouses.
But Ukraine’s partners did not provide the country with intelligence data from NATO’s early-warning satellites, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, as tensions between Washington and Kyiv rise.
He did not name the United States and President Donald Trump has denied that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence.
The constellation of military satellites detects Russian ballistic missile attacks by the rockets’ thermal flames seconds after launch.
The warnings give Ukrainians up to 10 minutes – precious, life-saving time to sound air raid sirens and send emergency text messages to prompt evacuations to bomb shelters.
“That’s what helps prevent the killings,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s ground radars can only detect the incoming missiles as their speed ranges from 6,000 to 12,000km/h (3,730 – 7,260 miles per hour).
‘Trump pressures our president’
Despite Trump’s denial, Ukrainian observers have a simple yet harrowing explanation – the US president wants to help Republicans win more congressional seats in upcoming midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv into declaring an “energy ceasefire” with Moscow that would drive global oil prices down.
“Trump pressures our president, pressures Ukraine” as he strives to “get advantage by any means necessary in the election campaign,” Lieutenant-General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s general staff of armed forces, told Al Jazeera.
The lack of intelligence data “significantly affects the effectiveness of air defence, we don’t have time to respond,” he said.
Without the satellite data, Ukrainian drones and missiles also “lose precision when striking targets deep in Russia,” he said.
On Sunday, Trump announced the ceasefire that envisages no mutual strikes on energy infrastructure – from Russian oil refineries and fuel depots to Ukrainian power and heating stations.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on social media.
Kyiv said the announcement was a surprise, while Moscow declined to say whether it backs the idea – and kept on hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The pressure goes beyond the refineries as Trump wants to quickly reopen, arbitrate and complete peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow – even if they benefit the Kremlin.
“He needs peace talks to succeed. Ideally, it is a certain unblocking of the peace settlement process, when Kyiv shows more willingness to agree with Russia’s demands,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.
The pressure will continue until “Kyiv shows readiness for a compromise and concessions towards Russia,” he said.
Moscow “simply abuses” the pressure and the suspension of air raid warnings to escalate attacks on Ukraine, he said.
Kyiv’s ‘priority’: The destruction of oil refineries
The suspension of data-sharing was especially shocking, given that Kyiv did stop hitting Russian refineries for three days.
It was only on Wednesday that its drones attacked refineries in Saratov and Ryazan regions, said Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksander Novak.
However, Kyiv’s focus on striking oil refineries is ineffective and counterproductive, another observer said.
“Kyiv’s strategic priority is still the destruction of oil refineries,” Nikolay Mitrokhin of Germany’s Bremen University, who has penned hundreds of authoritative analyses of the hostilities, told Al Jazeera.
However, Russia overcame the initial shock by transporting gas from refineries in Siberia and exporting it from neighbouring Belarus and Kazakhstan.
No economic collapse, massive joblessness or public protests followed the strikes, while Moscow continued its air raids, adding jet-powered drones that resemble cruise missiles and are hard to down with Ukraine’s existing air defence system, he said.
“What is the basis for Kyiv’s and its backers’ conviction that strikes on oil refineries and depots will lead to Russia’s strategic defeat before Ukraine is defeated? I don’t understand,” he said.
However, Ukrainian attacks on data centres, bridges and factories where drones are assembled are far more effective, he said.
Recent strikes on data centres of Russian online giant Yandex and the state-run Sberbank resulted in disruptions of services in Russia and even former Soviet republics where Yandex operates its online payment, food delivery and taxi services.
Trump “didn’t ask him to stop the war, to give away cities or stop striking Russian rears in general,” Mitrokhin said.
Kyiv has repeatedly reiterated that it was ready to start peace talks if they are preceded by a ceasefire, but Moscow wanted to continue ground assaults and air raids until the peace terms were finalised – which could take months or even years.
‘We’re ready for any turn of events’
On Wednesday, Ukraine’s drone czar accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite terminals that are part of the military-grade Starshield system.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said that SpaceX abruptly and without any warning limited services for terminals placed on drones flying over 160km/h (100mph).
The limit affected crucially-important interceptor drones and followed Trump’s request, presidential adviser Serhii Sternenko said.
Musk said that the White House owns and controls the Starshield systems and that any limits on speed are decided by Trump.
Some military analysts warn that the limit may be followed by a total shutdown of Starlink for Ukraine that could damage the quality of all military communications.
“But we were getting ready for everything,” Andriy Pronin told Al Jazeera. “We already know it may happen, that’s why we’re ready for any turn of events.”
In September 2022, Musk secretly ordered engineers to switch off Starlink coverage in the Russia-occupied Kherson region, effectively thwarting Kyiv’s push to retake it, Reuters reported.
In 2023, Musk threatened to cut off Ukrainian military access to Starlink unless the US defence department took over the costs.
Later, the Pentagon, Poland and other European allies took over the costs.

Sergei Naryshkin, head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, arrived in Kabul on Wednesday and met Taliban intelligence chief Abdul Haq Wasiq. Neither side has disclosed the purpose of the visit.
The visit comes as relations between Moscow and the Taliban continue to expand. Russia formally recognised the Taliban government in July 2025 after removing the group from its list of banned organisations.
Since then, Moscow has emphasised the importance of expanding political, economic and security cooperation with the Taliban.
Naryshkin is among the senior Russian officials who supported closer relations with the Taliban even before Moscow formally recognised its government.
At a conference on Afghanistan in Baku in April 2025, he praised the Taliban’s governance and said international recognition of its government was inevitable.
At the same meeting, the Russian intelligence chief accused Western countries of seeking to prolong instability in Afghanistan by keeping Afghan assets frozen and providing intelligence support to Taliban opponents.
On 18 October 2025, on the sidelines of a meeting of intelligence and security chiefs from Commonwealth of Independent States countries in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Naryshkin also expressed opposition to the establishment of foreign military bases in Afghanistan.
He said Afghanistan had always attracted the attention of international actors, but Russia’s position was clear: Afghanistan should remain an independent country without foreign military bases. He described this as being in the interests of regional countries and, above all, the Afghan people.
In June 2024, Naryshkin also said the Taliban was the only force capable of controlling Afghanistan’s territory.
He has previously praised the Taliban’s efforts against Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), saying the authorities in Afghanistan were making extensive efforts to combat the group.
Naryshkin’s visit to Kabul comes as Russia continues to express concern about security threats originating in Afghanistan, particularly the activities of extremist groups and the risk of instability spreading into Central Asia.
Moscow has repeatedly warned about the activities of ISKP in Afghanistan and called for greater regional cooperation to counter terrorist threats.
