ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers Kazakhstan’s partnerships with Azerbaijan and Belgium, proposed AI rules for newsrooms, and plans to expand Middle Corridor logistics infrastructure.
President Ilham Aliyev meets with Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and officially inaugurates Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable
President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev met with President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Oct. 15, reported Trend.
During the meeting, the sides hailed the successful development of the strategic partnership and allied relations between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan.
They highlighted the successful organization of the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, adding that the event had provided a good opportunity to discuss cooperation among countries in the Asian region.
Subsequently, Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Kassym-Jomart Tokayev officially inaugurated the Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Cable Line in an online format.
Kazakhstan weighs AI rules for newsrooms amid growing digital risks
Kazakhstan is considering new rules governing the use of artificial intelligence in newsrooms, including requirements to label AI-generated content. The proposal was discussed at the tenth Astana Media Week, which also focused on digital threats and children’s online safety, reported AnewZ on Oct. 15.
“Dmitriy Mun, CEO of Q.AI, predicted that AI could generate much of the content for some radio programmes and commentary within two to three years.
With automated content expected to become more common, Mun argued that the real challenge for journalists would be earning public trust rather than simply delivering information.
Fact-checking, accuracy and editorial independence could therefore become crucial in distinguishing professional journalism from machine-generated content,” reads the article.
Kazakhstan and Belgium to open new chapter in their partnership
EU Reporter published an article on Oct.12, written by Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Belgium Roman Vassilenko, exploring how the first Belgian state visit to Central Asia could strengthen Kazakhstan-Belgium ties through trade, investment, transport connectivity, and broader economic, academic and cultural cooperation.
“For Kazakhstan, relations with Belgium also have an important European dimension. Brussels combines bilateral diplomacy with dialogue with the European Union institutions. Transport connectivity, investment and resilient supply chains form a shared agenda in which Belgian expertise and Kazakhstan’s potential can, and do, complement each other,” reads the article.
Belgian royals in Kazakhstan: first state visit to Central Asia
Brussels-based VRT News released an article on Oct. 12 about the first-ever state visit to Central Asia by Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde, aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation with Kazakhstan in trade, critical minerals, technology, and science.
German logistics group Rhenus plans up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor
Global logistics company Rhenus Group plans to build a new multimodal hub in the Kazakh city of Aktau and develop up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor. This network will link Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Türkiye, and connect the route to the company’s infrastructure in Europe, reported Euronews on Oct. 9.
German logistics giant Rhenus Group is set to roll out a network of up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), with a new trimodal container terminal in Aktau.
Azerbaijan–Kazakhstan ties could reorient Central Asian integration
The five Central Asian presidents met with Azerbaijan’s Ilham Aliyev in Avaza on Oct. 8 for the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and the Republic of Azerbaijan, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 12.
Azerbaijan’s participation brings a principal outlet for Central Asian trade into the six governments’ economic deliberations. Within their consultative format, the states can coordinate industrial projects with the transport services through which regional producers reach foreign markets. If Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan connect cross-Caspian transport more closely to industrial cooperation, the corridor could become an organizing axis for regional integration.

articles.title: Afghanistan’s Road to Nowhere, and the Central Asian Way Around It - The National Interest
articles.summary: Afghanistan’s Road to Nowhere, and the Central Asian Way Around It  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
Central Asia’s investment in Afghanistan could reduce the region’s dependence on Russia without US recognition of the Afghan Taliban.
In early October 2026, the Afghan Taliban completed a 121-kilometer (75-mile) gravel road through the Wakhan Corridor, the narrow valley in Afghanistan’s far northeast that links the country to China. Afghan reports show that Kabul paid for it from the national budget, 365 million afghanis (about $5.5 million), with no reported Chinese investment.
Over three years, Kabul pressed Beijing to open a border crossing at the corridor’s end and bring Afghanistan into the Belt and Road Initiative. No Chinese representatives were reported at the opening, and Beijing has not announced that it will open its side. Trade through Wakhan would support Afghanistan’s economy and the Taliban administration’s standing, while China would gain a direct land route to the Afghan market and its mineral deposits.
While Taliban officials claim China aims to invest in joint infrastructure projects, Beijing has been more cautious. In January 2026, China’s state news agency Xinhua wrote that the corridor’s security situation is complex, that its elevation and climate make it impassable most of the year, and that opening a border crossing is unrealistic in the short term. Yet, China has already solved the terrain problem at the nearby Khunjerab Pass.
The obstacles lie on the Afghan side of the border. Beijing fears that militants could use an open corridor to reach Xinjiang. Chinese companies cannot reliably transfer profits from Afghanistan, and Afghan contracts have proven unreliable. Kabul’s conflict with Pakistan adds a political cost for Beijing. Until these problems are addressed, the new road will carry little trade. Meanwhile, Central Asia already offers China and other traders a working route into Afghanistan, and Washington has a stake in keeping it open.
Afghanistan’s Resources Have Nowhere to Go
Although much of the country remains unsurveyed, Afghanistan holds significant deposits of copper, iron ore, lithium, and rare earths. Its non-fuel mineral wealth has been estimated at more than $1 trillion, and its copper resources could rank among the world’s five largest if proven accessible. Little of this wealth has been exploited. The flagship Chinese project, the Mes Aynak copper mine, was awarded in 2007 but only entered development in late 2025, and in May 2026 Afghan authorities were still pressing the contractor to begin production.
Trade flows reflect the same problems. According to China’s Ministry of Commerce, China exported $1.544 billion of goods to Afghanistan in 2024 but imported just $42 million, down 34 percent from the year before, despite granting Afghan products duty-free access.
Xinhua’s terrain argument doesn’t hold up. China’s Khunjerab Pass, in Tashkurgan, the same county that borders Wakhan, sits at 4,733 meters (15,528 feet), comparable to the 4,923-meter (16,152-foot) Wakhjir Pass at the corridor’s end. Until 2024, Khunjerab closed every winter. Beijing approved year-round operation in May 2024 and opened it that December. The following month, cargo through the pass rose more than tenfold year over year, although from a low winter base.
China can keep a high-altitude crossing open year-round when what lies on the other side justifies the cost. Militant risk exists on the Pakistani side as well. In March 2024, a suicide bomber killed five Chinese engineers working on the Dasu dam. In return, Pakistan offers an army that guards Chinese projects and a banking system Chinese firms can use. Wakhan opens onto a country that offers neither.
Why Afghanistan Is Capital-Dry
After the Taliban’s return to power in 2021, Afghanistan was cut off from the international banking system, its central bank reserves were frozen, and foreign banks cut their correspondent relationships. Five years later, the banking sector remains fragile. The World Bank’s latest update names limited access to finance as a core barrier to private investment. China’s own Ministry of Commerce spells out what this means for its companies. No Chinese bank operates in Afghanistan, and dollars are often routed through Bank of China’s Dubai branch. There is no direct yuan-afghani settlement.
Sending money out of the country requires approval from Afghanistan’s central bank, which it generally does not grant, and repatriated dividends are taxed at 20 percent. Foreign firms cannot obtain local financing, and the two countries have never signed a bilateral economic agreement. Under these conditions, the cost and risk of doing business in Afghanistan are too high for most firms other than state-backed ones. Repatriation is only part of the risk.
Contracts offer foreign investors little protection under the Taliban administration. In January 2023, Taliban officials signed a 25-year contract with China’s Xinjiang Central Asia Petroleum and Gas promising $540 million in investment to develop oil fields in the Amu Darya basin. In June 2025, the deal collapsed, with the Taliban citing repeated contract violations. Chinese employees interviewed by NPR described something closer to expropriation at gunpoint and warned that foreign investors would stay away in such conditions.
Security adds to the deterrents. Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISIS-K), the Islamic State’s Afghan branch, claimed responsibility for the January 2026 Kabul restaurant bombing, which killed one Chinese national and six Afghans. China’s Commerce Ministry’s 2025 Afghanistan guide lists the East Turkistan Islamic Movement (ETIM) among militant groups active in Afghanistan; a UN Security Council monitoring report likewise records member state reporting of ETIM/TIP’s presence there.
The Pakistani Problem for Afghanistan
Kabul’s conflict with Islamabad further complicates the picture. Pakistan has long been the Taliban’s closest patron and is China’s key partner through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). In August 2025, the three governments agreed in Kabul to extend CPEC into Afghanistan, a framework that ties Afghanistan’s trade with China to Pakistani routes.
Two months later, Pakistan closed its Afghan border crossings, and in February 2026 the dispute escalated into military operations against the Taliban. Pakistani air raids on Afghan territory continued into October 2026. In March 2026, Beijing sent a special envoy to both capitals to mediate. Opening a direct route to Kabul now would look like taking sides and would weaken Pakistan’s role as Afghanistan’s main gateway to the sea.
Afghanistan’s Challenges for Investors
Taliban decision-makers hope the new Wakhan road will bring trade and foreign investment. Investors will look first at institutions. The Taliban administration would need a central bank that lets profits leave and courts that enforce contracts and protect foreign assets. It would also need tighter border security to assure Beijing that an open crossing won’t threaten Xinjiang. Few companies or governments will invest where their assets are at risk, and their money cannot leave.
Kabul cannot fix this alone. Correspondent banking and settlement depend on foreign banks, and the frozen reserves depend on foreign governments.
This gap gives Central Asia a role. Its states can act as intermediaries, letting Beijing trade with Afghanistan without opening its own border at Wakhan. Kazakhstan already carries Chinese goods to Afghanistan by rail, and Kazakh-Afghan trade reached $581.1 million from January to July 2026, up significantly from the previous year. Two Kazakh banks have started correspondent relationships with Afghan banks. Uzbekistan has gone further, establishing an escrow system through Ghazanfar Bank that pays Uzbek exporters once their goods reach the Afghan border. Central Asian banks can provide the financial plumbing that Chinese and other foreign traders need to reach Afghanistan.
Why Washington Should Care About Central Asian-Afghan Investment
American policymakers would rather not deal with Afghanistan, yet the country now matters to a region Washington cares about. The United States left Afghanistan because staying no longer served vital US interests. Central Asia has since gained weight in Washington as part of the Middle Corridor and as one of the fastest-growing regions tracked by the EBRD, with new data center investment arriving. Its governments are pursuing new partnerships, including with the United States, and reducing their dependence on Russia. Kazakhstan still sends more than 80 percent of its oil exports through Russia via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium. It now plans to generate more of its own electricity and is looking for export routes that bypass Russian territory.
Kazakhstan’s rail links to China are expanding, and Astana is shipping more oil west across the Caspian Sea. A southern route through Afghanistan would add access to South Asian markets and Pakistani ports. Astana has committed to the Turgundi-Herat railway and has signed a memorandum with Uzbekistan and the UAE to study a railway through Afghanistan to Pakistani ports. Russia, for its part, wants to become the outside power Kabul turns to first. It recognized the Taliban government in July 2025 and has courted it diplomatically since.
But if Central Asia continues to pursue economic relations with Afghanistan, the whole region can strengthen its independence from Moscow and become more resilient. Andrew Kuchins, senior fellow at the Center for the National Interest, reaches a similar conclusion in his July 2026 report, The Case for Deeper US Engagement with Afghanistan. He writes that all five Central Asian states are “far ahead of the United States” in their engagement with Kabul and can serve as “a very useful bridge for US policymakers and private sector actors.”
Washington once saw this clearly. The State Department’s 2019–2025 Central Asia strategy, released in 2020 when a US-backed government still ruled Kabul, pledged to “encourage c

articles.title: Zelenskyy blasts Trump’s diesel deal and calls Russian peace moves a ‘parody’ - Al Arabiya English
articles.summary: Zelenskyy blasts Trump’s diesel deal and calls Russian peace moves a ‘parody’  Al Arabiya English
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took aim on Friday at US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and welcomed the prospect of European allies stepping up their role in talks, calling Moscow’s stance a “parody” of peace negotiations.
At a European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy said Russia did not want peace. He added that Ukraine was still experiencing disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used for battlefield operations and to down Russian drones attacking cities far from the frontline.
For the latest updates on the Russia-Ukraine war, visit our dedicated page.
EU leaders rallied around Zelenskyy after Trump again criticized Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace.” On arriving at the summit, Zelenskyy pointedly referred to his counterparts there as “real leaders.”
The EU was hosting Zelenskyy at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
Nevertheless, Zelenskyy’s tone suggests he has little intention of softening his stance towards the US. Asked at a press conference whether he felt he was being used as a scapegoat by Trump for high energy prices and the trajectory of the Iran war, Zelenskyy paused for a long time, smiled, and said “this is my answer,” to laughter in the room.
‘Money in Putin’s pocket’
Trump blindsided Zelenskyy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. Facing US midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
His diesel deal with Russia angered Ukraine and European allies.
“And now we can see how cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal,” Zelenskyy told the press conference on the sidelines of the summit.
“This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets. But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
Zelenskyy also accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of not being interested in peace talks in any form.
“Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form,” he said. 
“He’s playing with words, claiming they respond... Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war.”
The Kremlin said last week that Ukraine had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of peace talks after it had hit Moscow with drones during last month’s election.
Meanwhile in the latest attacks in Ukraine, Russian drone strikes on the city of Kharkiv killed three people, while strikes elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.
In an interview, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.
“The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion ($79 million) more from you – for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskyy said in his address to the EU leaders, which he later posted on X.
“This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”
EU leaders grappling with budget
Ukraine’s leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the Starshield satellite system.
A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.
Zelenskyy said the operation had improved but not yet been fully restored, adding the disruption placed civilians at risk.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can’t replace this capability,” said the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelenskyy declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.
Russia has also publicly acknowledged the drone attack on a refinery and broadcast images on state media, breaking with its usual practice in order to play up the incident.
While EU leaders hit out at the US deal to buy Russian diesel, they are also grappling with how to tackle energy prices that have soared since the Iran war, exposing divisions between member states on day one of the summit on Thursday.
Splits continued on Friday, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson saying member states were “incredibly far apart” from each other when it came to finalizing the EU’s own budget. 
“There isn’t even a glimpse, as they say, a shred of agreement on this,” he said.

articles.title: Kazakhstan Proposes Regional Biodiversity Convention Office in Almaty at Global Summit - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Kazakhstan Proposes Regional Biodiversity Convention Office in Almaty at Global Summit  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed the establishment of a regional office for the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) in Almaty, positioning Kazakhstan as a central node for environmental diplomacy in Central Asia. The proposal was unveiled during the Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity in Yerevan, Armenia, which is being held on the sidelines of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention (COP17). The initiative signals Astana's ambition to lead regional efforts in combating habitat loss, managing transboundary water resources, and adapting to the severe impacts of climate change across the Eurasian steppe.
The Central Asian region is uniquely vulnerable to ecological degradation, facing a complex matrix of challenges that include the desiccation of the Aral Sea, the fluctuating water levels of the Caspian Sea, and the rapid melting of the Tien Shan glaciers, which serve as the primary water towers for millions of people downstream. By hosting a regional CBD office, Almaty would serve as a coordination hub for the five Central Asian republics—Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan—to harmonize their national biodiversity strategies and action plans (NBSAPs). This harmonization is critical for managing migratory species, protecting shared river basins, and securing international climate finance that often requires regional rather than bilateral approaches.
President Tokayev's address in Yerevan extended beyond institutional architecture to include specific technological and ecological interventions. He notably proposed the creation of a common digital platform designed to monitor and protect the Caspian Sea ecosystem. The Caspian, the world's largest inland body of water, is currently experiencing a alarming drop in water levels, a phenomenon driven by a combination of reduced river inflow from the Volga and increased evaporation rates linked to rising regional temperatures. A unified digital monitoring system would allow the five littoral states to share real-time data on pollution, sturgeon poaching, and hydrological changes, overcoming the historical opacity that has hindered cooperative management of the sea's resources.
The push for a regional environmental framework is not new, but Tokayev's elevation of the issue to the COP17 summit demonstrates a shift in Kazakhstan's foreign policy priorities. Astana has increasingly leveraged its role as a regional hegemon to mediate resource disputes, particularly concerning the transboundary waters of the Syr Darya and Amu Darya rivers. Tokayev has previously championed the idea of a Central Asian Framework Convention on Water Use, a proposed treaty that would legally bind the region to equitable water-sharing principles. The proposed CBD office in Almaty would likely function in tandem with such water agreements, recognizing that biodiversity conservation in arid Central Asia is inextricably linked to hydrological management.
The Kazakh steppe, one of the largest contiguous dry grassland ecosystems on Earth, is home to unique and highly endangered species such as the saiga antelope. Once hunted to the brink of extinction, saiga populations have made a remarkable recovery in recent years due to strict state protection, but they now face a new threat from climate change. Unprecedented winter snowstorms, known as "dzuds," followed by rapid spring thaws and summer droughts, are altering the vegetation dynamics of the steppe and disrupting the antelopes' migratory routes. A regional CBD office would be instrumental in coordinating cross-border conservation corridors, ensuring that these ancient migration paths remain viable as climatic zones shift northward.
International environmental observers have noted that the success of the Almaty proposal will depend heavily on the willingness of neighboring states to cede a degree of environmental sovereignty to a Kazakh-led institution. While the ecological imperatives for cooperation are undeniable, historical tensions over water allocation and border demarcation have occasionally strained relations within the region. However, the escalating frequency of climate-induced disasters, such as severe droughts and transboundary dust storms, is forcing a pragmatic recalibration. The presence of a UN-backed CBD secretariat in Almaty could provide the neutral, technical platform necessary to depoliticize these sensitive discussions and focus on data-driven mitigation strategies.
The realization of Tokayev's vision will likely require substantial backing from multilateral development banks, such as the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the World Bank, which have increasingly prioritized climate resilience in their Central Asian portfolios. These institutions have already funded various projects aimed at improving irrigation efficiency and restoring degraded pastures, but a unified regional strategy could unlock larger-scale concessional financing. By aligning the proposed Almaty office with the Global Environment Facility (GEF) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF), Kazakhstan could position itself as the primary conduit for international climate aid in the region, further solidifying its role as the indispensable broker for Central Asian development and environmental sustainability.
As COP17 progresses, the international community is watching to see if the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund can be mobilized to support such regional hubs. For Kazakhstan, the establishment of the Almaty office would not only enhance its diplomatic prestige but also attract significant technical expertise and green investment to a region that has historically been defined by its hydrocarbon wealth. Tokayev's proposal represents a strategic pivot toward a post-oil identity, one where the stewardship of the steppe's fragile ecosystems becomes a cornerstone of the nation's engagement with the global community. The coming months will reveal whether the international community is prepared to back this vision with the necessary institutional and financial support.

articles.title: Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Poland has scrambled its defences once again as Russian attacks overnight hit western Ukraine close to Poland’s border.
Poland’s armed forces said on Friday that they had scrambled fighter jets during the attacks and no violation of the country’s airspace was recorded.
It was just the latest such alert as Poland and other countries along NATO’s eastern flank grow increasingly concerned over the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine as Russia appears to be accelerating its tests of regional defences. Later on Friday, Bulgaria’s defence minister said Sofia has requested help from NATO to bolster its defences.
During air attacks across Ukraine overnight, numerous strikes hit the Volyn region, cutting electricity to 370,000 people across the western district, which sits on the border with Poland. Governor Roman Romaniuk reported that two people were injured.
In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a drone attack killed three people and injured five, the regional governor said. In central Ukraine, police said strikes on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number.
Private power company DTEK announced on Friday that it had implemented emergency power cuts across Kyiv due to ongoing strikes.
In Russia, officials said air defences had blocked a Ukrainian drone attack against a heating plant in the Vladimir region.
Ukraine has had significant success in attacking Russia’s energy infrastructure and its oil refineries in particular. However, that strategy has provoked anger from United States President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for pushing up global oil prices.
Russia said it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, 94 of them headed for Moscow.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said the capital’s four airports and St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport had suspended operations.
Ukrainian attacks killed two people in the Russian-controlled Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said.
Concern over Russian activity near NATO territory has grown since the summer as Romania, Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states reported numerous intrusions of drones into their airspace and waters.
That activity appears to be becoming more bellicose. In recent weeks, drones have struck at least seven cargo ships off the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, leaving 25 people dead or missing.
Drones hit two ships off Romania’s coast this week. A hit on a commercial vessel that sank off Bulgaria’s coast on Tuesday prompted Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Friday that while the evidence pointed to Russia, his government does not have proof.
Shortly afterwards, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters that Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and antidrone systems to bolster its defences.
“We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision,” Stoyanov said.
NATO did not immediately respond to a request for comment, the Reuters news agency reported.
Stoyanov said he plans to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO antidrone initiative by the end of October.
Romania’s president has also said that his country has asked for additional equipment.

articles.title: Russia’s stance a ‘parody’ of peace negotiations - The Daily Star
articles.summary: Russia’s stance a ‘parody’ of peace negotiations  The Daily Star

- Ukrainian attacks kill two in Russian-held Luhansk region
- Russia moves on local assets of more European firms
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky yesterday took aim at US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and welcomed the prospect of European allies stepping up their role in talks, calling Moscow’s stance a “parody” of peace negotiations.
At a European Union summit in Brussels, Zelensky said Russia did not want peace. He added that Ukraine was still experiencing disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used for battlefield operations and to down Russian drones attacking cities far from the frontline.
EU leaders rallied around Zelensky after Trump again criticised Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”. On arriving at the summit, Zelensky pointedly referred to his counterparts there as “real leaders”.
The EU is hosting Zelensky at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
On the eve of Zelensky’s appearance at the summit, Russia also moved to place local assets of French, German, Swedish and Dutch companies under temporary management, in retaliation for the EU’s support for Ukraine, reports Reuters.
Meanwhile, two civilians were killed as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine in the past 24 hours, the region’s Russian-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said yesterday.
Russian drones killed at least three people across Ukraine early yesterday, hit two shopping centres and knocked out power to around 370,000 in the northwest after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.
Ukraine has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, leaving it more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday. The source told CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”

Ukrainian forces reportedly regained unrestricted access to SpaceX’s Starshield on October 15, following in-motion speed restrictions on Starshield communications network over Ukraine. Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD) sources stated on October 15 that Ukrainian units are reporting the resumption of unrestricted Starshield access, following October 14 speed restrictions of 100 miles per hour (roughly 160 kilometers per hour) for the terminals connected to the Starshield communications network operating in Ukraine.[1] Starshield is a more secure, jam-resistant, and military-oriented version of the Starlink satellite network that SpaceX designed for government use, while Starlink serves civilian and commercial purposes.[2] Ukrainian forces do not have access to Starshield or any Starlink services over Russia as SpaceX has geographically restricted Ukraine’s access to just within Ukraine's international borders.[3] Ukraine therefore relies on alternative communication methods and point-to-point navigation to strike targets in Russia.
High-ranking Kremlin officials continue to emphasize that there is and was no energy ceasefire agreement, rejecting any meaningful concept of a ceasefire proposal. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov stated on October 15 that “there will be no ceasefire” in response to a journalist question about Russia’s willingness to make any concessions toward peace negotiations.[4] Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov additionally claimed that Ukraine did not adhere to a strikes moratorium against Russian energy facilities, amidst numerous reports that Russian forces continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure while Ukrainian forces refrained from striking Russian energy infrastructure between October 11 and October 14.[5] Peskov falsely claimed that Ukraine's and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's unwillingness to engage in peace negotiations is thwarting US peace negotiations efforts, attempting to paint Ukraine as the intransigent party in all wider peace efforts.[6] High-ranking Kremlin officials, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, have not offered any concessions in peace negotiations and have rejected numerous compromise proposals that both the US and Ukraine have offered, demonstrating the Kremlin’s continued unwillingness to compromise on any terms that fall short of fulfilling Russia’s maximalist demands of Ukraine’s complete capitulation.[7]
Ukrainian forces struck six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers at the Borisoglebsk Military Airfield in Voronezh Oblast overnight on October 14 to 15.
The Ukrainian Navy reported that Ukrainian forces used Neptune cruise missiles to strike the Borisoglebsk Military Airfield in Voronezh Oblast (roughly 267 kilometers from the international border) overnight on October 14 to 15, damaging six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers and technical equipment.
[8] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine’s strike against the Borisoglebsk Military Airfield destroyed four Su-34 fighter jets and damaged two more.
[9] Satellite imagery published on October 15 shows damage to four Su-34 fighter jets at the Borisoglebsk Military Airfield following a Ukrainian Neptune missile strike.
[10] A Russian milblogger responded to the strike by emphasizing that Russian forces need layered ground- and air-based air defenses to protect Russian aircraft close to Ukraine’s border.
[11] The milblogger noted that Russian forces can preserve their aircraft assets only by temporarily withdrawing all frontline, long-range, and military transport aviation beyond a 400-kilometer radius from Ukraine’s international border.
Russian forces routinely use Su-34M fighter-bombers to conduct missile and glide bomb strikes against Ukraine.
[12] The basing of Su-34M aircraft in close proximity to Ukraine’s border allows Russian forces to conduct more sorties during strike series, prolonging the aircraft’s engine life and consuming less jet fuel.
Ukraine’s ability to force Russian aviation farther away from the international border will increase Ukraine’s ability to detect Russian sorties sooner and mobilize air defenses faster, potentially helping to mitigate the more devastating impacts of cruise missile strikes.

Likely Russian drones struck four civilian vessels in the Black Sea, including two commercial tankers in Romanian territorial waters on October 14 and 15.
Romanian Foreign Minister Toiu Oana stated on October 15 that unspecified drones struck four commercial vessels, including within Romanian territorial waters and its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and noted that “Russia bears full responsibility” for those strikes.
[13] Reuters reported on October 15 that unnamed actors struck the San Marino-flagged Wine Trader tanker 13 nautical miles (roughly 24 kilometers) southeast of the Romanian Sulina Canal (one nautical mile outside of Romanian territorial waters) and the Comoros-flagged Yara J chemical and oil tanker eight to 10 nautical miles (roughly 15 to 19 kilometers) southeast of the canal within Romanian territorial waters on October 14.
[14] An unnamed NATO official told Reuters that the drones that struck the vessels "were of Russian origin.
"[15] A NATO statement added that unspecified drones also struck the Marshall Islands-flagged Sea Destiny bulk carrier within Romanian waters and the Tanzanian-flagged Dania J tanker, reportedly moored in Ukraine’s Izmail Port.
[16] Automatic identification system (AIS) data from the Starboard Maritime Intelligence ship-tracking platform indicates that Sea Destiny is currently anchored off the coast of Romania and Dania J was near the Izmail Port as of six days ago.
The strikes caused fires on board the Wine Trader and the Yara J tankers, leading to in-depth search missions and the ultimate rescue of five sailors, with seven sailors still missing.
Territorial waters extend up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometers) from the nation’s shoreline, compared to the EEZ which extends up to 200 nautical miles (roughly 370 kilometers) from the baseline, and states have sovereignty and jurisdiction over their territorial waters.
[17] Russian drone strikes against vessels in Romania's territorial sea violate Romania’s territorial integrity.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan declined to comment on Russia's involvement in the strikes as of October 15.
The October 14 and 15 drone strikes come against the backdrop of recent escalating Russian strikes against vessels in the Black Sea, including strikes against civilian vessels in the Bulgarian EEZ overnight on October 12 to 13.
[18] These strikes demonstrate Russia’s increasing willingness to pursue strike tactics that may directly impact the territory of NATO or NATO-aligned states.
